results.verdict: Oasis describes the most thorough PayPal integration on paper (Orders v2, server-side capture with amount checks, idempotency, verified webhooks, Payouts royalties, refunds), but the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', every proof number is a {{placeholder}}, only 9 tests back the testing claims, it isn't submitted to Devpost, and the store copies Polyfork's concept, copy and layout almost line for line, so a developer today can see a handsome storefront but cannot watch a single PayPal order get approved or captured.
fixes: Set the PayPal sandbox and Anthropic credentials on Render so /api/config returns paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then confirm the full path live: Buy now opens Smart Buttons, the buyer approves, the server captures and the licensed download unlocks. Prove the agent chat runs the same path from a brief.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real sandbox evidence: order IDs, capture IDs, payout batch IDs for a fork-of-fork split showing 60/30/10 to three sandbox accounts, a webhook event log (CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED, PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED, PAYOUTS-ITEM), and the refund count. Delete any number you can't back. Then actually submit on Devpost.

Record a 2–3 minute demo that shows each step without cuts: Claude via `/mcp` calls create_order and returns the payer-action link, the human approves in PayPal's window, get_order captures and returns downloads, and the royalty payouts appear in the sandbox dashboard. This is the agentic-commerce story that beat the field at Dev Days (CrawlerPal), and it is currently invisible.

Back the claims with tests and a doc a developer can learn from. Add tests for the capture amount/currency mismatch that triggers an auto-refund, webhook signature verification, the capture-lock race, the 799-cent royalty split and the QuickJS memory-bomb kill. Publish a PAYPAL.md walkthrough of the order→approve→capture→webhook→payout code. Also differentiate the hero and asset pages from Polyfork, so the original pieces (Brand Mode and the human-approved agent order) lead instead of the borrowed concept.

results.verdict: Oasis has a well-designed payment architecture on paper (idempotency keys, a capture lock, amount-checked capture, verified webhooks, a QuickJS sandbox killed from outside) and a polished but closely Polyfork-derived storefront, yet the live deployment shows paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page says it isn't configured, every proof number is still a {{placeholder}}, the factory log contradicts the grader claims, and the entry isn't submitted, so none of the agentic-payment story is demonstrated end to end.
fixes: Make the core flow actually work live. Set the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Anthropic key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then run and record one unbroken flow: brief, agent remixes, cart, PayPal order, human approval, server-side capture with amount check, licensed download, royalty payout. Link the video and give judges sandbox buyer credentials.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real numbers pulled from logs and sandbox order IDs, then submit on Devpost. Reconcile the visible contradictions or remove the claims: factory v2 logged 1 build with 0 rejections against a claimed grader reject rate, and the catalogue shows 41 built-in assets against 43 assets plus 3 forks.

Back the robustness claims with tests. Nine tests can't cover what the writeup asserts. Add tests and CI for: duplicate capture racing across browser, return URL and webhook with the same PayPal-Request-Id; amount or currency mismatch triggering an auto-refund; webhook signature failure being rejected; the refund webhook revoking a licence; payout failure and retry; the cent-exact royalty split along a fork chain; and the sandbox escape and worker-kill cases.

Harden agent-initiated payments beyond 'a human approves'. Enforce the brief's budget cap on the server before create_order. Rate-limit and attribute the unauthenticated MCP create_order calls. Show the requesting agent and the itemised remix in the order description. Log an audit trail per order. Also give the UI an identity that doesn't mirror Polyfork's hero copy and layout line for line.

results.verdict: Oasis is a polished storefront that knowingly copies Polyfork's model, but its PayPal pitch is not proven: the live server reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', every proof number is still a {{placeholder}}, only 9 tests exist and 1 factory-v2 build is logged, and the entry is unsubmitted, so today it is claims plus nice screenshots.
fixes: Make the core loop work on the live URL: configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude agent. Then record an unedited video that goes from brief to branded kit to the PayPal approval window to capture to licensed download, plus one fork-of-fork Payouts split. The agent-creates-order, human-approves flow is your only real differentiator from Polyfork, and right now a judge cannot see it.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real, verifiable numbers: orders captured, payouts, refunds, assets, knobs and grader rejection rate. Link them to /api/stats or sandbox transaction IDs. Delete or soften any claim you can't back, such as broad test coverage when only 9 tests exist, or factory scale when only 1 v2 build is logged.

Get outside evidence of demand before the deadline: a handful of real users or external MCP keys making calls, a few paid (even sandbox-to-live) licences, and one creator whose fork earned a royalty. Polyfork wins on 54 paying customers and $4,428, while you have zero users.

Submit on Devpost and reframe the story around PayPal, not Polyfork. Lead with the agentic-commerce primitive: server-priced orders, the capture lock, webhook recovery, auto-refund on amount mismatch, and lineage royalties via Payouts. Show the approval UI, and keep the 'Polyfork for 2D' framing to one line.

results.verdict: Oasis has a beautifully crafted, Polyfork-shaped storefront and a sharp agent-proposes/human-approves PayPal idea, but the live site has PayPal and the agent switched off (paypalReady:false, agentReady:false, 'The agent isn't configured on this server'), the write-up is still full of {{placeholders}}, and it isn't submitted, so nothing that would make it a PayPal winner is proven.
fixes: Make the core loop work on the live URL. Configure the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Anthropic key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then run real briefs through agent, remix, PayPal approval, capture and licensed download, and publish a sandbox buyer login so judges can complete a checkout themselves.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with numbers you can show, and reconcile what you have against what you claim. Currently there are 41 built-in vs 43 assets, 9 tests, and 1 factory-v2 build. Link captured order IDs and payout batch IDs, or cut any claim (royalty payouts, refunds, grader reject rate, sandbox-escape tests) you can't back up today.

Record a 2–3 minute video and submit to Devpost. Show Brand Mode recolouring the catalogue, then the agent building the Tidepool kit and rejecting its own render. Show PayPal's approval window, the capture, and the 60/30/10 payout split landing for a fork-of-a-fork. Finish with an external Claude client using /mcp from create_order to get_order.

Make the asset store look like its own product rather than a Polyfork re-skin, and make the agent page useful even when the agent is unavailable. The headline, 'Exports to' strip, 'How it works' and 'Use it' layout map nearly one-to-one onto Polyfork. Lead the hero with the brand-plus-PayPal-approval story instead. Replace the empty agent pane with a replayable recorded session showing the renders, the cart and the PayPal order.

results.verdict: Oasis describes a textbook-correct PayPal integration (server-side capture with amount checks, idempotency keys, verified webhooks, Payouts royalty splits, refunds), but none of it is proven: the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', every PayPal number is still a {{placeholder}}, 2 of 21 tests fail, the entry is unsubmitted, and the visuals and copy track Polyfork so closely that the only original parts (agent-initiated, human-approved PayPal orders and fork royalties) are exactly the parts that cannot be demonstrated.

Then run the full flow live: create order, approve, server capture, verified CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED and PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED webhooks, and a Payouts batch for a fork-of-a-fork. Publish the real order, capture and payout batch IDs, and replace every {{placeholder}} with those measured numbers.

Record a 2-minute video of the core claim. An agent brief (in-app and via the /mcp create_order tool) produces a branded kit and a payer-action link, a human approves in PayPal's window, and the server captures and issues licences. Show the 60/30/10 royalty payouts arriving in the sandbox accounts.

Make the claims and the evidence match. Fix the 2 failing tests and state the real count. Reconcile the writeup's factory claims (lessons, reject rate, 40-asset v1 run) with the verified log of 1 factory v2 build, or cut them. Add a short developer-facing README section with the capture-lock, amount-verification and webhook-verification code, so other PayPal developers can learn from it.

Stop shadowing Polyfork and lead with what is PayPal-native. Replace the near-copy hero line ('Design assets you can reshape') and the isometric-town showcase with the agent-proposes, human-approves PayPal checkout and the upstream royalty chain. Then submit on Devpost with a working live link.

results.verdict: Oasis describes exactly the payment hardening I would want (server-side capture, amount checks, idempotency keys, a capture lock, verified webhooks), but none of it can be confirmed: the live server reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server,' 2 of 21 tests fail, every headline number is still a {{placeholder}}, and the polished storefront closely tracks Polyfork's copy and diorama look.

Fix the 2 failing tests. Add integration tests against the sandbox for the claims that matter: duplicate capture with the same PayPal-Request-Id, browser/return-URL/webhook capture racing on one order, auto-refund on amount or currency mismatch, rejection of a webhook with a bad signature, and licence revocation on PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED. Publish CI results instead of the unverified '{{tests}} tests' line.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real numbers from logs, or delete the claim. Reconcile the inconsistencies: 45 vs 42 assets, a 'factory v1' of 40 assets vs 1 logged v2 build, and the grader reject rate and payout counts. Unproven metrics read as fabrication to judges.

Submit on Devpost with a 2-minute demo video, and lead with what Polyfork and Countersign don't have: Brand Mode across the catalogue, plus agent-initiated PayPal orders with fork-chain royalty payouts. Add a visible spend cap and an 'order created by agent X' summary in the approval step so the human-approval story is shown working, not just asserted.

results.verdict: Oasis has a well-reasoned PayPal design (agent creates the order, human approves it, forks pay royalties upstream) and a clean remix UI, but the live site has paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, 2 of 21 tests fail, every proof number is still a {{placeholder}}, the hero copies Polyfork's, and it has no users, so today it is a polished Polyfork clone whose payments story is only a claim.
fixes: Make the core loop real on the live URL. Configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the agent so that /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true, then record an unedited 2-minute run covering: brief → branded kit → PayPal approval window → server capture → licensed download → a fork royalty payout visible in sandbox. The agent page currently opens on 'The agent isn't configured on this server,' and a judge will stop there.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real, linkable numbers: orders captured, payouts sent, refunds, grader reject rate, dead knobs found, test count. Fix the 2 failing tests and actually submit on Devpost. Factory v2 has logged 1 build, so either show the factory's real volume or drop the claims about it.

Get outside evidence of demand before judging. Examples: 5–10 real people or external agents completing sandbox purchases, logged MCP calls from keys you don't own, and a quote from a builder who used an Oasis asset in a v0 or Lovable project. Polyfork wins on 54 paying customers, not on its pitch.

Differentiate from Polyfork on the first screen. Drop the cloned 'X you can [verb]' hero and isometric town. Lead instead with what only Oasis does: Brand Mode re-skinning the whole catalogue, an agent proposing a cart, a PayPal approval card naming which agent asked, and a fork-royalty split diagram. On the agent page, swap the error state for a one-click sample brief.

results.verdict: Oasis is a polished but derivative 2D take on Polyfork, and its PayPal-hackathon centrepiece is absent from the live site: the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', /api/config reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the write-up still contains {{placeholder}} metrics, 2 of 21 tests fail, and the Devpost entry is unsubmitted.
fixes: Put the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Anthropic key on Render so paypalReady and agentReady both return true. Then run the full flow on the live URL: brief, agent remix, PayPal approval, server capture, licensed download. Publish sandbox buyer credentials so judges can complete it themselves. Right now the core feature shows an error banner.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real counts from actual sandbox runs: orders captured, payouts sent, refunds, renders per asset, grader reject rate, tests. Fix the 2 failing tests. Reconcile the inconsistent numbers: 45 assets in the API vs 42 built-in, and the factory claims vs 1 logged v2 build. A judge reads unfilled braces as 'never happened'.

Record a 2–3 minute video of that one end-to-end path. Include the agent discarding a bad render, PayPal's approval window, the capture, and a fork-of-a-fork licence triggering visible 60/30/10 Payouts to three sandbox accounts. Link the video and the live URL at the top of the README and the Devpost entry, then submit.

Stop leading with an isometric low-poly town that reads as a Polyfork clone. Make Brand Mode the home-page hero: one brand picker re-rendering a grid of icons, cards and posters live. Next to it, show the 'agent proposes, human approves in PayPal' flow. Those two things are what Oasis has that Polyfork doesn't.

results.verdict: Oasis describes a textbook PayPal integration (Orders v2, server-verified capture, request-id idempotency, signature-verified webhooks, refunds, and Payouts royalties down a fork chain), and its storefront is polished, but the live server reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the Agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server,' the entry is unsubmitted, and the concept and visuals closely follow Polyfork, so the headline flow cannot be demonstrated and it ranks behind R1, R5 and the live-demoed R2.
fixes: Make the demo run. Set the PayPal sandbox secret and the Claude key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Remove the error banner from the Agent page, publish sandbox buyer credentials in the submission, and record a 2-minute video of the full flow: brief, agent cart, PayPal approval window showing the agent name and spending cap, server capture, licensed download, payout.

Prove the PayPal depth with artefacts instead of prose. Add a public sandbox order/receipt page and a webhook event log showing CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED, PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED and PAYMENT.PAYOUTS-ITEM.* events with real sandbox order, capture and payout-batch IDs. Link each one from PAYPAL.md next to the code it exercises, so a developer can learn from it and a judge can verify it.

Fix the royalty and refund model. Paying Payouts 'the moment payment is captured' while offering 14-day refunds leaves creators paid on refunded licences. Hold payouts until the refund window closes, or document how payouts are clawed back. Also state plainly that real creator splits belong on PayPal Commerce Platform (multiparty, platform fees) rather than Payouts, and build or stub that path.

Submit on Devpost, freeze the build, and reconcile every number before judging. The write-up says 48 assets, the live config says 49 and the repo has 52 built-in. The factory log shows 19 builds and 11 published, which sits awkwardly with 'most of the catalogue was written by an agent pipeline.' Then sharpen differentiation from Polyfork around what only Oasis does: the brand-role system and the agent-creates, human-approves PayPal order.

results.verdict: The PayPal engineering on paper is exactly what I want to see: server-priced verified capture, a single capture under races, PayPal-Request-Id on create, capture and refund, verified webhooks and 22 passing tests on tampering and the cap, but the live deployment reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', and the Devpost is unsubmitted, so the core agent-to-PayPal flow cannot be verified end to end, and the visual concept leans heavily on Polyfork.
fixes: Set the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude key on Render so /api/config shows paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then run and record one complete sandbox purchase through the live site: agent brief, cart, order creation, approval in the PayPal window, server capture, webhook and licensed download. A PayPal track cannot be judged on a checkout that is switched off.

Submit on Devpost with a demo video of that flow and the MCP path. The video should show create_order rejecting a total above max_total_usd, the agent name appearing on the PayPal approval screen, get_order capturing and returning downloads, a forced amount mismatch that triggers an auto-refund, and a refund webhook that revokes the licence.

Fix the money-movement gap in royalties. Payouts sent at capture cannot be recovered when a refund arrives inside the 14-day window, so the platform eats the loss. Hold royalty payouts until the refund window closes, or net them against later earnings, and add a test for refund-after-payout. Also make the agent page degrade to a recorded sample run instead of an empty error state.

Add an automated end-to-end sandbox test in CI covering order create, approve, capture and the webhook, and publish its output. Reconcile the inconsistent numbers (48 vs 49 vs 52 assets). Sharpen the differentiation from Polyfork and Countersign around Brand Mode and fork-lineage payouts rather than reusing the isometric-town and knobs presentation.

results.verdict: Oasis frames agentic commerce correctly (the agent creates the order, the human approves it, the server enforces the cap), but its headline feature is dead on the live site (paypalReady:false, agentReady:false, and the agent page says 'The agent isn't configured on this server'), it has no users or numbers, it is not submitted, and it reads as a polished Polyfork reskin with a PayPal layer bolted on.
fixes: Turn on the sandbox PayPal credentials and the Claude key on Render so the agent and checkout work live. Then record a 90-second demo that runs unbroken: brief, branded kit, agent's reasons per licence, PayPal approval window showing the agent name and cap, capture, licensed download. Without this, the PayPal story is unproven.

Submit on Devpost with that video and a screenshot of the actual PayPal approval screen. Unsubmitted means zero, and the agent-can-ask-but-not-pay moment is the one thing judges from PayPal need to see.

Replace claims with evidence, even small: N real sandbox orders, M external agents calling /mcp (log Claude Desktop or Cursor sessions), one real fork chain with a live Payouts royalty split shown in the sandbox dashboard, and a handful of named users who made a kit.

Reconcile the numbers (48 vs 49 vs 52 assets, 479 knobs) and differentiate from Polyfork. Lead the homepage and story with the payments primitive (spending cap, human approval, fork royalties via Payouts) and with Brand Mode, not with the borrowed isometric town and knobs framing.

results.verdict: Oasis is a crisp, carefully engineered and openly Polyfork-derived store whose PayPal design (server-verified capture, idempotency, webhooks, spending cap, fork royalties via Payouts) is the most thoughtful on paper, but the live site has paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the Agent page literally says 'The agent isn't configured on this server', and the Devpost isn't submitted, so its headline claim is unproven where a judge would click.
fixes: Turn the live demo on. Configure the PayPal sandbox credentials and the agent key on Render so a judge can type a brief, watch the kit fill, approve in PayPal's sandbox window and download the licensed remix. If API cost is the worry, add a rate-limited demo brief or a replay of a real recorded session as a fallback. Never ship the yellow 'not configured' banner.

Submit the Devpost with a 2-minute video of the full loop. Show brief → agent rejecting its own render → branded kit → PayPal approval showing the agent name and cap → server capture → fork-chain Payouts landing ($6/$2/$1/$1). Include sandbox transaction IDs and an MCP client (e.g. Claude Desktop) shopping via /mcp.

Make every number consistent and checkable. The README says 48 assets and 479 knobs, the live API says 49, the catalogue says 52, and the factory log shows only 19 builds with 11 published. Pick the true figures and link the factory verdict log, test output, and the harness's dead-knob report.

Put the differentiators above the fold on the homepage instead of a Polyfork-style isometric hero. Add a live Brand Mode demo that re-skins several assets at once, the agent-asks/human-pays flow, and a copy-paste MCP config. Add a 'How it works' strip so the site argues for itself rather than reading as Polyfork in 2D.

results.verdict: Oasis describes the deepest PayPal integration in this field: Orders v2 with server-verified capture, idempotency, signature-verified webhooks, refunds that revoke licences and refund-gated Payouts, all covered by 23 passing tests, but the live server reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent only replays a recording, the Devpost entry is unsubmitted, its numbers are already stale against the logs (47/22/25 builds claimed vs 55/23/32 logged, 66 vs 64 assets), and the core concept and visuals closely follow Polyfork, so a judge cannot yet watch the one thing that makes it a PayPal project actually work.
fixes: Configure PayPal sandbox credentials on the Render deployment so /api/config shows paypalReady:true. Publish a sandbox buyer login in the README so a judge can complete create order, approve in PayPal, server capture and licensed SVG/PNG download on the live site in under two minutes.

Turn the live agent and the MCP checkout path on, using a hard server-side cap and rate limit. Record an unedited video of an MCP client calling create_order with max_total_usd, a human approving in the PayPal window with the agent's name visible, and get_order returning the licence. This replaces 'Watch a real recorded run' with something verifiable.

Publish a public /proof page fed by real sandbox events: a PayPal order ID, its capture ID, a verified CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED and PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED webhook log, and a Payouts batch ID splitting a fork-of-a-fork royalty in exact cents. Either wire PayPal Commerce Platform multiparty (payee plus platform_fees) now, or say clearly that Payouts is a sandbox stand-in.

Submit on Devpost and stop committing. Regenerate every number in the writeup from the live catalogue and factory log so assets, forks and build counts match /api/config and PROOF.md. Sharpen the difference from Polyfork with one 2D-specific proof, such as Brand Mode re-skinning one real customer's kit in a single PayPal order.

results.verdict: Oasis has the right PayPal primitives on paper: server-priced verified capture, idempotent create/capture/refund, signed webhooks, a server-enforced spend cap and a sandboxed renderer, plus a polished store that matches Polyfork visually. But the live deployment reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page falls back to a recorded run, the Devpost is unsubmitted and the writeup's counts disagree with the repo, so none of the agent-to-PayPal flow can be verified end to end and it trails Polyfork and Countersign.
fixes: Configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the agent key on the Render deployment so /api/config reports paypalReady and agentReady as true. A judge should be able to run brief, cart, create_order under the cap, approve in PayPal, server capture and licensed download live, including through the public /mcp endpoint.

Submit on Devpost with a short unedited video of a real sandbox run. It should show the agent name and cap on PayPal's approval screen, a closed-tab capture via the CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED webhook, an amount-mismatch auto-refund and a refund revoking the licence.

Generate every number in the writeup from source and freeze the repo before judging. The writeup says 66 assets and 47/22/25 factory builds, but the repo shows 64 built-in assets and 55/23/32 builds, and the last commit landed 30 seconds before review. Mismatched self-reported metrics cost credibility with a payments reviewer.

Harden the payment path beyond 23 unit tests. Add a sandbox-backed end-to-end suite covering the full flow, MCP cap bypass attempts and replayed or forged webhooks. Either ship the Commerce Platform payee/platform_fees split now or demonstrate one real held royalty payout with a refund cancelling it.

results.verdict: Oasis is a well-engineered and visually coherent store with a correct agentic-payments model (the agent creates the order, the human approves in PayPal, the server enforces the cap), but it closely follows Polyfork's concept, factory and visual language while showing none of Polyfork's traction, and on the live site paypalReady and agentReady are both false and the Devpost entry is unsubmitted, so a judge cannot run the core PayPal flow.
fixes: Make the core loop runnable for a judge today. Enable PayPal sandbox credentials and the agent on the live deploy so paypalReady and agentReady are true. A judge should be able to go brief → branded kit → PayPal approval screen showing the agent name and spending cap → capture → licensed download. Add a 2-minute video of that run and submit the Devpost entry.

Replace claims with evidence of demand. Report real numbers: external agents calling /mcp, distinct users who ran a brief, sandbox or live orders approved, and creators who forked and got paid. Even small, honest numbers beat zero against a reference with 54 paying customers and $4,428 in revenue.

Differentiate from Polyfork on the PayPal side, because the store, knobs, factory, grader and diorama art are all borrowed. Lead the homepage and demo with what is new: the agent proposes and the human approves, with the per-item reason shown in PayPal; the server-enforced cap; and the fork-of-a-fork royalty chain paid by Payouts and held through the refund window. Show a real payout ledger for one chain.

Fix the trust and UX gaps. Reconcile stale numbers (the writeup says 47/22/25 factory builds but the log shows 55/23/32; config reports 66 assets but the catalogue has 64 built-in). Replace the agent page's 'live agent is resting' line with an auto-playing recorded run. Fill the empty space below the homepage hero with a how-it-works section and a mock of the PayPal approval screen. Put the Licence buy button above the fold on asset pages.

results.verdict: Oasis is a well-crafted, honestly engineered take on Polyfork's programs-as-assets idea, with a real PayPal twist: the agent creates the order and the human approves it. Generate every number in the README from the same source as PROOF.md and freeze the build before judging. The README says 66 assets and factory v2 at 47/22/25, while the live check shows 64 built-in and 55/23/32; stale numbers undermine the 'measure the artefact' pitch.

Publish sandbox buyer credentials so a judge can run the full path live: brief, branded kit, order under the cap, approval in PayPal, server-side capture, licensed download.

Submit the Devpost with a 2-3 minute unedited video of a live run. Show the PayPal approval window displaying the agent name and cap, a webhook-driven capture after closing the tab, a deliberate amount-mismatch refund, and a refund revoking the licence.

Prove the MCP path with real artefacts. Connect an external agent such as Claude Desktop to /mcp, attempt a create_order above max_total_usd and show the server refusing it, then complete one under the cap. Commit the real sandbox order, capture, refund and payout IDs with their verified webhook events to PROOF.md.

Harden agent-initiated payments beyond 23 tests. Add rate limiting and abuse controls on the unauthenticated /mcp create_order, webhook replay/duplicate-delivery tests, and an end-to-end Playwright test against the PayPal sandbox in CI. Either implement the Commerce Platform payee/platform_fees split or test the Payouts hold-and-cancel path against the sandbox rather than only in unit tests.

results.verdict: Oasis has the right PayPal primitive for agentic commerce (the agent creates the order, the human approves it, the server enforces the cap) and a disciplined build log, but it is an unsubmitted Polyfork-for-SVG with no users or revenue and a live site where both PayPal and the agent are switched off, so it currently proves less than the winners it has to beat.
fixes: Turn on paypalReady and agentReady in the live deploy so a judge can run the whole flow themselves: brief, branded kit, PayPal sandbox order showing the agent's name and the cap, approve, capture, licensed download. Also post a 90-second video of that exact run with the PayPal approval screen visible.

Bring evidence of demand, because right now there is none. Get real people and external agents to use it, then publish the counts: MCP calls from external keys, sandbox or real orders captured, and a few named testers who branded a kit. Polyfork wins on 54 paying customers, and Oasis has zero.

Rebuild the agent page around its payoff. The replay screenshot shows a near-empty chat and an empty kit and checkout. Open on the finished state (four branded assets, itemised cart, cap meter, PayPal button), then let the replay explain how it got there.

Submit on Devpost, and sharpen the why-pay story against free shadcn/Figma kits and image generation. Lead with a one-click Brand Mode before/after on your own palette, and prove the royalty chain with a real sandbox Payouts batch ID and webhook trace. That also helps the visuals, especially the isometric town, read as more than a Polyfork reskin.

results.verdict: Oasis is a well-crafted, honestly documented Polyfork-for-2D with a sharp agent-proposes, human-approves PayPal primitive, but the live site has both PayPal and the agent switched off (paypalReady:false, agentReady:false), the agent 'replay' screenshot stalls on one search step with an empty kit, and nothing is on Devpost yet, so its strongest claims are still unproven to a judge.
fixes: Turn the live deploy on: set the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude key so paypalReady and agentReady are true. Let a judge run a real brief through to PayPal's approval window, showing the agent name and spending cap, then capture and download. Until then, make the replay finish within about 10 seconds: a filled 'Your kit' panel and a visible PayPal button, not a mostly empty chat.

Submit to Devpost with a 2-minute video of one unbroken take covering five steps: the Tidepool brief, the agent rejecting a muddy render and remixing, the branded kit, PayPal sandbox approval and capture, and a fork-of-a-fork sale producing three sandbox Payouts. Put the order IDs and payout batch IDs in PROOF.md.

Make the differentiation from Polyfork visible above the fold rather than buried in the README. Show Brand Mode as a before/after strip on the home page: paste a palette and watch the whole browse grid re-skin. Add a short 'agent can ask, can't pay' diagram, because the hero isometric town currently reads as a Polyfork homage.

Prove the MCP endpoint is usable by outside agents. Add a copy-paste Claude Desktop/Cursor config snippet on the For AI page and a public counter of real /mcp calls. Include one recorded third-party agent session that ends with create_order and a human-approved capture.

results.verdict: On paper this is the most thorough PayPal integration in the field: Orders v2 with server-priced verified capture, PayPal-Request-Id idempotency, signature-verified webhooks, refunds, and Payouts for fork royalties, all backed by 25 passing tests. But the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page is a replay, and the Devpost entry is unsubmitted, so a judge cannot complete a single PayPal approval on what is, visually and conceptually, a 2D reskin of Polyfork.
fixes: Put PayPal sandbox credentials on the Render deployment so /api/config returns paypalReady:true, then publish sandbox buyer credentials in the README. A judge should be able to run create order, approve in PayPal's window, server capture, and licensed download on the live URL in under a minute.

Turn on the live agent and the MCP create_order path behind a rate limit and a low global cap (agentReady:true). A judge's own brief should return a real payer-action link instead of a replayed transcript. The agent-proposes, human-approves flow is the whole PayPal pitch, and right now it cannot be exercised.

Submit to Devpost with a 2-3 minute video of one unedited sandbox run: the agent builds the kit, the order shows the agent name and cap, the PayPal approval popup appears, then capture, a CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED or PAYMENT.CAPTURE webhook in a visible event log, and a Payouts batch ID for a fork-of-a-fork royalty. Show the real sandbox order, capture and payout IDs on screen.

Make the creator split PayPal-native now rather than 'in production': use multiparty per-unit payee plus platform_fees in sandbox, or at least show the held-then-released Payouts flow end to end. Add a public /paypal status page listing recent sandbox orders, webhooks and payouts. That turns PAYPAL.md from a claim into something a developer can verify and learn from, and gives Oasis a PayPal-specific edge over Polyfork.

results.verdict: Oasis has the right payments design on paper: agent-created orders, human approval, a server-enforced cap, verified capture with auto-refund on mismatch, PayPal-Request-Id idempotency and signed webhooks, but the live deploy reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page is a replay, and Devpost is unsubmitted, so nothing PayPal-related can be verified end to end and it trails Polyfork's real revenue and Countersign's depth of tested spend controls.
fixes: Configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude key on the Render deploy so /api/config shows paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. A judge must be able to brief the agent live, approve in PayPal's sandbox window, see the server-side capture and download the licensed SVG, without relying on a recorded replay.

Submit on Devpost with a 2–3 minute video of one unbroken flow: an outside MCP agent calls create_order with max_total_usd, a server-side refusal when the cart exceeds the cap, the human approves, get_order captures, and a refund webhook revokes the licence. Show the sandbox order and capture IDs on screen.

Add end-to-end evidence beyond 25 unit tests. Run Playwright against the PayPal sandbox for create, approve, capture and refund. Replay duplicate and out-of-order webhooks against the deployed endpoint. Run a concurrent-capture test against the live service. Publish the run log in PROOF.md with order IDs.

Make the royalty story honest and verifiable. Either run a real sandbox Payouts batch after a simulated refund window and show the PAYMENT.PAYOUTS-ITEM status tracking, or state plainly that the split is simulated until Commerce Platform onboarding, so the most novel claim ('forks pay upstream') doesn't rest on assertion.

results.verdict: Oasis has the most thorough PayPal integration on paper and a polished, coherent store, but the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page is only a replay, Devpost is unsubmitted, and there are no users, so it reads as a well-engineered Polyfork remake for design assets plus an agentic checkout that a judge cannot actually run.
fixes: Make the live demo work end to end: configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude agent on oasis-design.onrender.com so a judge can type a brief, watch the cart fill under the cap, click through PayPal's approval screen showing the agent name, and download the licensed kit. Then replace the 'replay' banner with a live run.

Submit on Devpost with a 2-minute video. Make the PayPal moment the climax: the order created by an outside MCP agent, the payer-action link handed to the human, approval, server-side capture, and a fork royalty showing up as a Payouts item. Link the sandbox transaction IDs.

Replace claims with external evidence. Get even 10–20 real outside users or agents to complete sandbox orders. Get a few third-party creators to publish forks. Publish real MCP call counts from keys you don't own, the way Polyfork did with its 14,524 calls from 29 keys.

Lead with what Polyfork doesn't have and stop echoing its visuals. Put Brand Mode and 'the agent asks, you approve in PayPal' above the fold instead of an isometric town that mirrors Polyfork's diorama. Clean up the agent screen's confusing 'recorded run / your cart is untouched' state so the spending cap and the approve step are the obvious hero.

results.verdict: Oasis is a well-crafted, coherent store with a sharp agentic-commerce angle, but it currently fails its own PayPal hackathon test: the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page is a replay, and the Devpost entry is not submitted, so its strongest PayPal claims rest on a README and passing unit tests rather than anything a judge can click through.
fixes: Configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. A judge must be able to brief the agent live, see the cart, and complete a real sandbox PayPal approval and capture that ends in a licensed download.

Submit the Devpost entry with a 2–3 minute video. It should cover the full loop in one take: a brief, the agent rejecting a muddy render, the PayPal approval window showing the agent's name and cap, server capture, and the download. Add a short clip of an outside agent shopping over /mcp.

Add a visible judge path on the home page: 'Try it in 60s' with sandbox buyer credentials and a pre-filled brief. Pair it with live receipts for the parts only Oasis has: a refused over-cap order, and a fork-of-a-fork sandbox payout split with real PayPal transaction and payout IDs. The concept and visuals closely track Polyfork, so the PayPal approval flow and royalty mechanics are the only clear differentiators and need visible proof.

Tighten the agent page. Stream the actual remix renders inline in the chat instead of leaving a large empty pane under four search chips, and drop the 'Replay' banner once it runs live. Then put the 25 passing tests, factory pass and reject stats, and PROOF.md on a public status page linked from the nav, so evidence sits next to the claims.
